line/points: Describe each image by two numbers, called its features: say, how much blue it has, and how many straight edges. Then every image is a point on a graph. Cats land low and to the left; ships, with sea and masts, up and to the right.
line/line: Telling them apart means drawing a line between them. You know a line from school as y equals m x plus b: m tilts it, and b slides it.
line/rewrite: Here both directions are features, so the same line is written another way: every point x where w dot x, plus b, is zero. The weights, w, do what m did, and b is the same b.
line/rotate: Change the weights in w, and the line turns.
line/slide: Change b, and it slides without turning. Set b to zero, and the line is pinned to the corner where both features are zero: no line through there splits these. b moves it out between them.
line/side: Plug a point in, and w dot x plus b is its score. A ship at three, three: three plus three, minus four, is two. A cat at one, one scores minus two. Positive on one side, negative on the other, and bigger the farther from the line.
line/linear: Features times weights, added up, plus b: a straight line. That is why this is called a linear classifier.
rows/x: Now three classes, cat, dog and ship, and an input x with features two and one.
rows/W: Each class gets its own line: its own weights, and its own bias. Stack the weights as rows, and they make a matrix, W: one row per class, one column per feature.
rows/row: Each class scores the input with its own row. Cat's row is one and two. Dot it with x: one times two, plus two times one, is four.
rows/all: Dog's row gives one, and ship's gives five. That is all W times x does: one dot product per row.
rows/col: Always a row, never a column. A column holds one weight per class, three of them here, so it does not even line up with the two features.
bias/b: Then each class adds its bias, b, one number per class: one, zero, and minus two.
bias/s: The scores, s equals W x plus b, come out five, one and three. Cat scores highest, so the classifier says cat.
bias/forget: Leave the bias out, and ship wins instead, with five. The bias is part of the score, not an afterthought.
bias/zero: Set x to all zeros, and W times x vanishes. The scores are exactly b: each class's lean before it sees any evidence.
bias/name: That lean gives the bias its name: it tilts a class's score up or down before any evidence, the way a bias tilts a judgment.
bias/why: It is the same b that slid the line. Without it, an input of all zeros would score zero for every class, so every class would start level. With it, a class that turns up often, like cat, can start ahead.
